 3 weather alerts in effect USDA proposal would end SNAP eligibility shortcut used by Alabama 
 By Gillian Brooks Published : Nov. 12, 2026 at 5:14 PM CST | Updated : 1 hour ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BIRMINGHAM, Ala. ( WBRC ) - A possible change to eligibility could leave thousands in Alabama without access to SNAP benefits.
 The U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed earlier this week to limit automatic eligibility.
 The proposal would end a shortcut that states like Alabama use to qualify families for SNAP, called broad-based categorical eligibility.
 If the rule is finalized, some families who qualify now will have to qualify under current guidelines. Some of those families would lose their benefits.
 Right now, families who receive certain noncash services through Temporary Assistance for Needy Families - or TANF - can automatically qualify for SNAP benefits.
 The proposal would change the broad-based categorical eligibility policy that allows states to use TANF services, like child care or job training, to qualify families for SNAP, even if they exceed the program’s standard income limit.
 Latrell Clifford Wood, a hunger policy advocate with Alabama Arise, said the change would affect some households.
 “The impact would be that households with maybe a car that’s broken down that’s worth more than $4,000, will no longer be eligible for SNAP simply because of that vehicle,” said Wood.
 Wood said he is concerned the changes could put more work on the Department of Human Resources (DHR).
 “This would increase the amount of items that our Department of Human Resources has to verify and increases the chance of increasing the error rate,” Clifford Wood said.
 Clifford Wood said families concerned about losing their benefits if the new rule is passed should stay informed and know what they are eligible for.
 “It’s really important to talk to your DHR agent during your interview process, like your phone interview to ensure that you aren’t losing benefits that you’re eligible for,” Clifford Wood said.
 A public comment period is open until Dec. 10.
